title: Why Three Precisions
narration: Now let's see why the paper uses three precisions. Look at the table on the board. Each row is a job in one Newton step, and each column is a precision. [[show_res]]First, the residual F of x is computed in double precision. It is cheap, because a fast Fourier transform does it in about N log N work, and it sets the accuracy we finally reach. [[show_jac]]Second, the Jacobian is stored in single precision. Building it costs only about N squared work, and single precision roundoff is about six times ten to the minus eight, which is small enough to behave like double. [[show_fact]]Third, the factorization is done in half precision. This is the expensive part, about N cubed work, so it is the part where cheaper arithmetic saves the most. [[hl_fact]]Take N equal to 4096. N cubed is huge compared with N squared, so the factorization dominates the cost. [[show_ir]]Half precision alone is sloppy, so iterative refinement repairs the step, using the single precision Jacobian to compute residuals. The result matches Newton with a double precision Jacobian, except for very ill conditioned problems, where GMRES with the half precision factorization as a preconditioner rescues it.

objects.text: Iterative refinement fixes the half precision step
